original_title: Rubio Admits Iran MOU Violated Within Two Weeks — Cannot Articulate War Endgame

sources.title: Secretary of State Marco Rubio Remarks to the Press
sources.access_notes: Official transcript supports the July 19 economic remarks, diplomatic comments, and stated military objective; it does not support the MOU-admission or endgame claims.

sources.title: Trump, Vance, Iran’s parliament speaker signed MOU, Reuters reports
sources.access_notes: Separate June reporting about the memorandum does not attribute a later two-week violation admission to Rubio.

supported_facts.fact: On July 19, 2026, Rubio described Iran’s economy as being in shambles, discussed severe inflation and shortages, said diplomacy would be positive if Iranian factions favoring it gained influence, and stated the U.S. military objective concerning attacks on commercial shipping.
Reuters separately reported a June U.S.-Iran memorandum; that is a distinct event from Rubio’s July remarks.

unsupported_original_claims: Rubio admitted Iran violated the MOU within two weeks.
Rubio could not articulate a clear war endgame.
CNN reported an internal administration split from a July 1 segment tied to the alleged admission.
access_notes: The original combines July 19 remarks with separate June MOU reporting and a July 1 CNN segment. The official transcript is accessible; no reviewed source directly supports the claimed two-week admission or inability to state an endgame.
narrow_corrected_title: Rubio describes Iran’s economy and policy in July remarks
narrow_corrected_claim: Rubio describes Iran’s economic conditions, a possible diplomatic opening, and the stated U.S. military objective in July 19 remarks.
exact_gap: No exact source found for Rubio admitting an MOU violation within two weeks or failing to articulate an endgame; do not merge the June MOU reporting into his July remarks.

original_title: CAP Analysis: SNAP Coverage Losses Could Cause 70000 Deaths by 2040

sources.title: SNAP Cuts Could Lead to 70,000 Avoidable Deaths
sources.access_notes: The accessible analysis attributes a modeled projection to CAP; its publication date is March 19, 2026, not May or July.

supported_facts.fact: CAP estimated that SNAP cuts associated with expanded work requirements could lead to approximately 69,600 avoidable deaths by 2040, using projected participation reductions and prior research; this is a model, not an observed toll.

unsupported_original_claims: The cited analysis was published in July 2026 or on the record date of May 30, 2026.
The modeled deaths are an observed outcome or a certain forecast.
Brooke Rollins’s claimed celebration, unemployment comparison, and 1.6% fraud-rate claim are established by this CAP source.
access_notes: CAP’s publication date is March 19, 2026, so it does not match the stored May 30 date or synopsis claim of a July analysis. The source supports CAP’s estimate only; it does not substantiate the separate Rollins, unemployment, or fraud assertions.
narrow_corrected_title: CAP models potential deaths from SNAP cuts
narrow_corrected_claim: The Center for American Progress estimated that SNAP cuts could contribute to about 69,600 avoidable deaths by 2040; the figure is a conditional model attributed to CAP.
exact_gap: Keep the event date tied to CAP’s March 19 publication. Separate or remove the Rollins, unemployment, and fraud claims unless independently sourced.

original_title: Medicaid Eligibility Enrollment Rule Blocked: 1.3 Million Dual-Eligibles at Risk

sources.title: The Impact of H.R. 1 on Two Medicaid Eligibility Rules
sources.access_notes: Accessible KFF analysis summarizes final-law provisions and CBO estimates; it treats two delayed rules together.

sources.title: Medicaid Changes in House Reconciliation Bill Would Increase Costs for 1.3 Million Low-Income Medicare Beneficiaries
sources.access_notes: Updated note distinguishes the House-passed estimate from the enacted law.

supported_facts.fact: The enacted 2025 reconciliation law delayed specified provisions in both the 2023 Medicare Savings Program rule and the 2024 Eligibility and Enrollment rule until 2034.
KFF, citing CBO, reports roughly $122 billion in combined federal savings over ten years and about 400,000 more uninsured people in 2034 for the two-rule delay.

unsupported_original_claims: The final law’s E&E-rule moratorium alone is projected to cause exactly 1.3 million dual-eligible beneficiaries to lose Medicaid.
The $121.9 billion figure is attributable to only the E&E rule.
The House-passed estimate is the enacted law’s final estimate.
access_notes: The 1.3 million figure comes from analysis of an earlier House bill. The final-law figures cover delayed provisions in two rules together; the source does not establish exactly 1.3 million Medicaid losses under the final statute.
narrow_corrected_title: Reconciliation law delays two Medicaid eligibility rules
narrow_corrected_claim: The 2025 reconciliation law delayed provisions in two Medicaid eligibility rules; KFF reports CBO projections of about $122 billion in combined savings and 400,000 additional uninsured people in 2034.
exact_gap: Do not present the earlier House bill’s 1.3 million estimate as the final law’s effect or attribute the combined fiscal projection to one rule.

original_title: DOGE Fires 400 FAA Workers During Active Aviation Safety Crisis

sources.title: FAA fires fewer than 400 workers, transportation chief says
sources.access_notes: Reuters reporting distinguishes FAA probationary dismissals from a DOGE review.

sources.title: FAA firings raise safety concerns among aviation workers
sources.access_notes: AP coverage reports the union’s account of affected support jobs; it does not establish DOGE executed the dismissals.

supported_facts.fact: Fewer than 400 probationary FAA workers were dismissed in February 2025; Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said controllers and critical safety personnel were not among them.
Aviation union representatives said some dismissed support roles—including aeronautical information, maintenance, telecom, and flight-operations jobs—were important to safety.

unsupported_original_claims: DOGE itself fired the employees.
Thousands of FAA workers were dismissed.
Air traffic controllers or safety-critical employees were confirmed among the dismissed staff.
access_notes: The sources establish FAA probationary dismissals and a separate DOGE visit/review, not that DOGE executed the firings. Duffy’s account and the union’s account differ on the safety significance of affected support roles.
narrow_corrected_title: FAA dismisses fewer than 400 probationary workers
narrow_corrected_claim: The FAA dismissed fewer than 400 probationary workers in February 2025; the union said some dismissed support positions had safety-related duties.
exact_gap: Attribute the dismissals to FAA/administration actions as reported; do not attribute them to DOGE without direct evidence or imply controllers were fired.

original_title: Offshore Drilling Expansion: Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic Opened to Oil Leases

sources.title: Interior Launches Expansive 11th National Offshore Leasing Program to Advance U.S. Energy Dominance
sources.access_notes: Official release describes a proposed program and says potential sales are not final.

sources.title: 11th National OCS Oil and Gas Leasing Draft Proposed Program: First Analysis and Proposal
sources.access_notes: Official proposal text lists 34 potential sales in Alaska, Gulf, and Pacific areas and expressly omits Atlantic planning areas.

supported_facts.fact: On November 20, 2025, Interior released a draft proposal for the 2026–2031 offshore leasing program with up to 34 potential sales across Alaska, the Gulf of America, and the Pacific.
The draft proposal does not include Atlantic planning areas, and inclusion does not guarantee a future sale.

unsupported_original_claims: The January 20 order itself opened Atlantic, Pacific, and Arctic waters to lease sales.
The November proposal included Atlantic areas or finalized lease sales.
The proposal proves specific drilling leases were issued.
access_notes: The source supports a later draft national program, not the record’s conflated January 20 claim. Its proposal omits Atlantic areas and remains preliminary; it does not establish completed leases or sales.
narrow_corrected_title: Interior proposes offshore lease sales in Alaska, Gulf, and Pacific
narrow_corrected_claim: Interior’s November 2025 draft proposed up to 34 offshore lease sales in Alaska, Gulf, and Pacific planning areas; Atlantic areas were not included.
exact_gap: Separate January 20 executive-order policy from the later leasing-program proposal; describe the latter as a draft and omit Atlantic inclusion.

original_title: Virginia Giuffre Recruited by Maxwell as 16-Year-Old Spa Attendant at Trump's Mar-a-Lago

sources.title: Deposition of Virginia Giuffre
sources.publisher: U.S. District Court for the Southern District of New York (CourtListener RECAP)
sources.access_notes: Deposition transcript is accessible as a court-record PDF; Giuffre corrected the approximate meeting period to summer 2000.

supported_facts.fact: In her deposition, Virginia Giuffre described meeting Ghislaine Maxwell while working at Mar-a-Lago and said the meeting occurred in summer 2000, correcting an earlier estimate of 1999.

unsupported_original_claims: The meeting is established as occurring in 1999.
Giuffre was definitively 16 at the time based on this deposition.
The record proves what Trump knew about Maxwell’s conduct.
access_notes: The court deposition corrects the timing to summer 2000 and contains inconsistent age references. It documents Giuffre’s account of recruitment at Mar-a-Lago but does not establish Trump’s knowledge.
narrow_corrected_title: Giuffre says Maxwell recruited her at Mar-a-Lago in summer 2000
narrow_corrected_claim: Virginia Giuffre testified that Ghislaine Maxwell recruited her while she worked at Mar-a-Lago, placing their meeting in summer 2000.
exact_gap: Correct the event year and omit the precise age unless a consistent contemporaneous record supports it; do not infer Trump’s knowledge from location alone.

sources.title: Moody’s Downgrades U.S. Rating to Aa1 from Aaa
sources.access_notes: Moody’s release dates the downgrade May 16, 2025.

sources.title: Moody’s downgrades U.S. rating to Aa1 from Aaa
sources.access_notes: Reuters reports the downgrade and White House response by communications director Steven Cheung.

supported_facts.fact: Moody’s downgraded the U.S. sovereign rating from Aaa to Aa1 on May 16, 2025.
The contemporaneous political response cited in Reuters came from White House communications director Steven Cheung, who criticized the downgrade as political.

unsupported_original_claims: Trump personally made the quoted attack on Moody’s.
Analysts in these sources said that dismissing the warning compounded investor concerns.
access_notes: The evidence supports the downgrade and a White House response, but not personal attribution to Trump. The proposed record should identify the actual speaker and retain no unsupported paraphrase as a Trump quotation.
narrow_corrected_title: White House criticizes Moody’s U.S. downgrade
narrow_corrected_claim: Moody’s lowered the U.S. credit rating to Aa1 on May 16, 2025; White House communications director Steven Cheung criticized the decision.
exact_gap: The specific Trump statement described in the frozen claim remains unsourced; use the identified White House response or exclude personal attribution.

sources.access_notes: Reuters reports remarks in a March 30 NBC interview, not a late-August rally.

unsupported_original_claims: The cited statement was made at a late-August 2025 rally.
Trump told supporters to demand that he remain indefinitely or claimed a legal entitlement to a third term in the terms given by the frozen synopsis.

narrow_corrected_claim: Trump said in a March 30 NBC interview that he was not joking about a third-term possibility.
